recABS9cTyYGHFXEG.Body: The Sonic Slider is the flagship tool behind Biofield Tuning itself, a weighted tuning fork hand-tuned to 93.96 Hz, the twelfth harmonic of the Schumann Resonance, Earth's own natural electromagnetic pulse. Its extended handle lets you glide it smoothly across the face, neck, and body, and practitioners and users regularly report support for relaxation, circulation, and nervous system regulation. It's the same fork Chance uses in his own sessions, and a great entry point if you want to bring this work into your own daily routine.

rec7Vm5QNrDbc9sdb.Bio: Chance Garton is the host and producer of the Innerverse Podcast, where for over a decade he has investigated consciousness, mythology, symbolism, terrain health, and the psychosomatic language of the human body and mind. A biofield tuning practitioner, he uses tuning forks to help clients resolve physical symptoms, break negative patterns, and return to energetic coherence.
rec7Vm5QNrDbc9sdb.Name: Chance Garton
rec7Vm5QNrDbc9sdb.Role: Host of the Innerverse Podcast, biofield tuning practitioner & researcher

recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Bio: Kyle Denton is a community herbalist and medicine maker from Wisconsin who founded Tippecanoe Herbs with his wife Serena Marinelli in 2015. From their Milwaukee apothecary they craft small batch remedies from locally harvested and organic herbs, working from a bio terrain philosophy that blends Ayurveda with Western herbalism. He also runs Root Radical Herbal Academy, has taught for over a decade through his annual three season class and his Milwaukee herb walks, and sees clients as the Tuning Herbalist, using tuning forks to read the biofield. His Substack and podcast, Resonature, explore the interval between vital herbalism, biofield tuning and cosmology.
recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Name: Kyle Denton
recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Role: Community herbalist, founder of Tippecanoe Herbs

fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The alternative is the native", "body": "Chance Garton opens by taking apart the word alternative. What the culture calls alternative medicine, he argues, is actually the native thing, while the allopathic system is the alter native, taking what nature gave, inverting it, and handing it back as poison called medicine. He also refuses the phrase side effects, saying side effects are simply effects. That framing sets up the whole conversation with Kyle Denton of Tippecanoe Herbs, whose Milwaukee shop forages its own plants, works with local farmers, and makes every medicine it sells in an apothecary kitchen behind the counter."}, {"title": "Foundations instead of memorized uses", "body": "Kyle Denton describes spinning his wheels early on, memorizing that peppermint is for an upset stomach. His breakthrough was learning foundational energetic patterns rather than plant to ailment pairs. He came up through an Ayurvedic training, translating Vata, Pitta and Kapha back into air, fire, earth, water and ether, then overlapped that grid onto Western herbalism, Greek medicine and the four humors, Appalachian folk medicine and Native American practice. Now he asks a person whether their complaint feels hot or cold, tense or loose, dry or damp, and matches it to a plant that heats, cools, dries or moistens."}, {"title": "The map is not the terrain", "body": "The conversation keeps circling a single idea, that language is a map and the felt quality is the terrain. Chance Garton argues that an inverted culture puts the name before the feeling, so people cannot know a plant without a label and an authority to supply it. Kyle Denton agrees but adds a yes and, since categorizing is a real human gift and the scaffolding of names is useful once the feeling comes first. His teaching aim follows from this. He does not hand students authority, he reminds them they already carry it."}, {"title": "Kronos, Kairos and the wobble in the year", "body": "Chance Garton floats a suspicion that time does not run in perfect cycles, that a year may not be exactly 365.25 days and that nature carries wiggle. He borrows the Greek pair Kronos, measured clock time shown by the sky clock, and Kairos, subjective felt time. Kyle Denton confirms it from a decade of annual herb walks, including an Earth Day walk cancelled by a foot of snow, and pictures the calendar as an oval rather than a circle. Enslavement, they conclude, only happens when Kronos is placed ahead of Kairos."}, {"title": "Reading the young lung tincture", "body": "Kyle Denton walks through the young lung tincture he sent Chance Garton, and through the doctrine of signatures Paracelsus named around 1511. Elecampane, read as Helen of the Campania, dispels green and yellow mucus and suits those who feel foreign or unable to speak. Rosemary and osha are fellow aromatics, each with a different major. New England Aster, yellow centered with purple rays that open and close, relaxes the diaphragm. Plantain heals mucosal tissue and Solomon's seal acts as a gentle activator. Nature, he says, reuses patterns the way Rupert Sheldrake described morphic fields."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Kyle Denton is the head hippie in charge of potion preparation at his family company, Tippecanoe Herbs. Join us to discover the doctrine of signatures in the patterns of plants, to know through consciousness the virtues of vegetation without the need to memorize Latin names and categories.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension we talk about Kyle's philosophy for herbal blends and different dosages, astro-aromatics and the scents of Aries, using the spirit of the plant for medicine without needing the physical, and many more vital ideas.
